This study presents a novel dynamic time-series model called TD-PAR, a Poisson autoregressive with a key modification to incorporate time-varying parameters. We introduce a new specification for the TD-PAR model, where the underlying structure is defined by a stochastic process with constant mean. We further develop an estimation approach for TD-PAR, utilizing a stochastic gradient descent algorithm with a random walk prior to analyze the time-varying components. We conduct a theoretical analysis of the model, deriving expressions for the probability density function of the posterior distribution and the model's expected loss. We also develop an R package called tdpar to facilitate TD-PAR's implementation. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness by applying it to real-world datasets and comparing it to alternative time-series models, highlighting its advantages in terms of forecast accuracy and model fit.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

Numerous configurational molecular sampling methods, including MD, TDLA and HDLA, are evaluated based on their performance when employed with BD to tackle complex molecular dynamics simulations. The results indicate that both TDLA and HDLA yield precise configurations at a given time point, whereas HDLA is more efficient due to its ability to provide precise configuration values at the outset. Furthermore, HDLA demonstrates a stronger potential to overcome free fall modes of oscillations compared to TDLA. The research findings are supported by theoretical analyses and confirmed by multiple case studies involving Lennard-Jones systems in various states and configurations.

In order to improve image description generation systems, a rating task was performed with 13,145 descriptions on 80k images, resulting in a refined score that closely mimics how humans would assess these descriptions. This refined score, along with other metrics, was then used to evaluate three different approaches to training these systems: (1) using refined scores in addition to existing measures of accuracy, (2) using a variety of existing measures of accuracy, and (3) utilizing a diversity objective that helps descriptions sound unique. According to the obtained results, incorporating refined human feedback led to descriptions that are more coherent and less prone to overusing common terms, ultimately contributing to a creation of a human-centered evaluation metric that prioritizes clarity over novelty.

A novel approach has been taken to explore the relationship between conformal field theory and Euler-Arnold equations. Beginning with the general principles of CFT, a new connection is established to the equations of Euler-Arnold, specifically through the Poisson-Gordon equation and its applications. This newfound link enables a deeper understanding of how FK-conformal field theory corresponds to Euler-Arnold equations, opening up possibilities for further research and applications in dynamics, integrable systems, and geometry.

Based on an extension of the standard model where a new, heavy gauge boson is introduced, we predict the properties of potentially heavy baryons and mesons consisting of ordinary matter that could be observed at future colliders or in experiments exploring exotic particles. Since this new gauge boson interacts via weak force, its discovery is unlikely in near-future experiments, but it may be found in experiments using high-energy lasers to create plasmas similar to those produced in supernovae explosions or explosive stellar events that forge heavy elements. If discovered, this new gauge boson would signify the presence of heavy baryons and mesons that could be searched for using variants of existing theoretical models or by exploring new theoretical frameworks that incorporate hidden local symmetries.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDED systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.

This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for fitting probability density functions, specifically designed to accurately model quark and gluon distributions within particles. Due to the complexity of the underlying theoretical models, particularly in perturbative QCD, a detailed discussion is provided to ensure that the described methods are fully applicable to all relevant fitting tasks. The framework's utility is demonstrated by applying it to four distinct PDF fitting tasks, ranging from simple linear least squares fitting to more sophisticated regression models that account for collinearity and nonlinear behavior. A brief overview is also given for a companion computer code, titled 'pdf-fitter', which is released in conjunction with this paper to serve as a publicly accessible resource for the benefit of the scientific community.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. It modifies the Poiseuille flow prediction, resulting in a non-linear relationship between stress and strain. The theoretical model can be presented in two forms: initial or fundamental; and derived constitutive. The initial format is advantageous for applying the theory to physical phenomena, as it provides a direct connection between gravitational field and geometric operator. The fundamental frame plays a crucial role in nonlocal gravity physics, influencing how the theory is applied and interpreted. The nonlocal gravity theory may be applied to physical phenomena, starting with the simplest linear scenario, such as long-wavelength fluctuations, and ending with more complex scenarios, like the relationship between stress and strain in Poiseuille flow. The transition from the fundamental to derived constitutive relation is essential for analyzing nonlocal gravity through laboratory-based experiments.

This paper discusses the potential uses of minor systems in the LHC, particularly in conjunction with the main detectors. Since the main detectors will be fully occupied with the most significant collisions, minor systems are proposed to exploit less intense beams that could be used for various purposes such as measuring magnetic field strengths, verifying quantum mechanics, and conducting novel physics research. The proposed schemes include using lasers to measure beam energies, employing fixed-target modes to study proton structure, and utilizing magnetic fields to create polarized protons. Additionally, the paper explores the idea of using minor systems to investigate specific physics phenomena, such as CP violation in neutrino oscillations, and analyzing the feasibility of converting the LHC into a neutrino beam. The contribution of minor systems to the overall scientific output of the LHC is expected to be significant, with the potential to answer numerous important physics questions.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries, especially those in a low-mass variety, exhibit outburst recurrence intervals that are too short to have been detected by the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. Contradicting this idea, our research found that about 20% of low-mass neutron star binaries with high masses exhibit recurrence intervals exceeding a decade when viewed from the Earth, while about 50% of those binaries with outburst intervals less than a decade remain unknown to the Fermi telescope. These findings challenge the current understanding of the source nature within the Milky Way's center and suggest that further study is necessary.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often requires the representation of objects from one group directly adjacent to those from another, assuming a limited number of intermediate objects are involved. Determining if such a visualization is possible based on given constraints is a well-known problem in graph theory. We modify this problem to determine if, within a given maximum number of intermediate objects is involved in the visualization, objects from one group directly connect to objects from another group that meet specific properties. We categorize objects based on their involvement in the visualization and solve the main problem as a subproblem of determining the first (or last) object from one group that participates in the visualization meeting the defined property. This revised problem we believe is the first instance of its kind to be analyzed from a computational perspective. We develop an algorithm to solve this problem, demonstrating its efficiency by confirming it operates within a polynomial bound of the input parameter, specifically the number of objects from one group, and is thus feasible for use in fixed parameter tractability applications.

As the number of cores in CPUs continues to increase, power consumption and heat dissipation pose significant challenges. A promising solution is to explore the feasibility of reducing operating frequencies beyond the current GHz range to the MHz range, which was previously considered impractical due to performance degradation. This research proposes a novel framework, HyperDegrade, which involves dynamically shifting frequencies between critical sections of code to effectively utilize the benefits of low-frequency operation while minimizing performance losses. Through a combination of hardware and software optimizations, HyperDegrade successfully enables CPU functioning at GHz-to-MHz frequency gradients for the first time, demonstrating a 30.4% average power reduction with only a 2.4% average performance decrease on a wide range of benchmarks consisting of 1000 applications following a commonly used evaluation methodology.

We introduce a new algorithm in the rational identity calculus that effectively disentangles the welded link diagram representing a braid, by banishing all positive crossings in the process and leveraging the existence of an inversion move.

In cooperative systems with limited computation and communication capabilities, coordination and decision-making are crucial for achieving shared goals. This study explores a new perspective on this concept, focusing on a network of robots that carry out multiple tasks in an optimal and coordinated manner. It is assumed that the robots can only communicate with their immediate neighbors in the network, and that each task is represented by a linear function that the robots must determine through computation and communication. To solve this problem, a two-part process is proposed, beginning with an efficient method to determine the optimal linear strategies for each task based on the available information, and then using these strategies to determine the optimal action for each robot in each time period as a response to changing environmental conditions. This proposed approach is mathematically formulated and proven to be effective, and is presented in a simple and clear manner for robots to compute and communicate it with one another.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian product breakdown methodology.

The upgrade of advanced LIGO and Virgo interferometric detectors to their plus-minus plus-minus configuration aims to enhance sensitivity in the high-frequency range. By utilizing the resonant cavity's sloshing mode, these optimized designs can further improve signal-to-noise ratio for certain gravitational wave events, specifically those produced by binary neutron star mergers. For a signal with an amplitude of 10^-19 str, the improved signal-to-noise ratio is anticipated to be around 6 times greater than the current top-down and side-by-side configurations. Moreover, the sloshing-Sagnac design offers several benefits over traditional interferometric setups, including increased signal output and better noise performance when dealing with optical parameters.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. In such systems, the process of discovering available channels is critical, especially when a large number of devices are involved. A new discovery method called 'XL-MIMO Random Access Protocol' has been proposed, utilizing the visible region of signals as an innovative way to prioritize device assignments and optimize the signal strength. The article examines how the shape and size of visible regions are randomly distributed among devices and how this randomness affects the overall protocol performance. The research finds that the irregular distribution of visible regions leads to an overestimation of overall signal strength, contributing to the degradation of protocol efficiency. The authors develop a more accurate model predicting the signal strength and provide guidance on optimizing the protocol parameters to enhance performance.

The resurgence of interest in n-gram language models has been spurred by recent advancements in neural language models and various applications in text processing. This research investigates the potential of using neural language models as a foundation to train n-gram language models, with the goal of improving n-gram model performance and understanding the effectiveness of residual learning. Experimental results using datasets from the TREC Web Track and the Google Web Dataset have shown that neural language models can serve as an effective base model for training n-gram language models, with n-gram models consistently outperforming neural models in query-based ad-hoc retrieval experiments. The findings suggest that the size of the context window has a positive impact on retrieval performance, with larger windows yielding better outcomes; however, this trend was found to cease when the window size exceeded 20. The research indicates that pre-trained neural language models can be utilized to quickly train n-gram language models, with a significant reduction in training data requirements. This convenient training method allowed for the creation of n-gram language models for large datasets like the Google Web Dataset, which is a significant contribution to the community.

This investigation seeks to explore whether an system of automatically scanning ballot marks, using an image recognition technology, poses a risk of being manipulated or compromised, with the potential to alter election outcomes. To assess this risk, the researchers conducted a series of tests on a sample of 2.5 million fictional ballots, varying in number from 1 to 10 marks per ballot, with each mark representing a different issue. The tests aimed to determine if the system could be tricked into misinterpreting or altering the marks on the ballots. Various scenarios were explored, including attempting to erase, change, or add marks on the ballots, as well as testing the system's ability to distinguish between actual marks and artificial ones, such as those created with makeup or temporary tattoos. A video game character with an 'X' marked through their eye was also used to see if the system could be fooled by an image that might resemble a cross-shaped mark. The research found that the system was susceptible to being deceived in several instances, including when a ballot with a mark made using temporary tattoo paste was scanned alongside an ordinary ballot. However, it's essential to note that these findings do not imply that any real-world election outcomes have been affected or that the system's vulnerabilities could be exploited remotely. The researchers stress that their discoveries highlight the importance of implementing additional security measures, such as using paper ballots and conducting thorough risk assessments, to ensure the integrity of elections.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.

This study formulates integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function, incorporating a parameterization that arises from a specific extension of the Bernoulli distribution. Consequently, we derive a normalized integral expression for the reciprocal gamma function by utilizing this distribution's generating function. Moreover, we utilize the relationship between the gamma and reciprocal gamma functions to obtain a representation of the reciprocal gamma function in a normalized form following a specific power function.

This paper formulates a hydrodynamic theory to describe interacting Bose gases within a phase-space random field approach, thereby incorporating both macroscopic hydrodynamic and microscopic quantum fluctuations into the model. A key advantage of this formulation is that it omits the need to solve the Schr\"odinging equation for individual particle dynamics, instead describing the quantum behavior through the Wigner function and its evolution according to a hierarchy of equations. To facilitate the application of this approach, we derive a linearized equation for the Wigner function that takes the form of a linear partial differential equation, along with a conserved energy momentum tensor to utilize in hydrodynamic calculations. Furthermore, we work out the specific details for a uniform, stationary state of the gas to demonstrate the implementation of the phase-space hydrodynamic theory within the condensed matter quantum field theory toolbox, especially utilizing the Monte Carlo method to perform numerical simulations.

Deep Neural Networks have excelled in various areas of knowledge learning, primarily in games like Go, Poker, Robotics, and Complex Strategies like Chess. Nevertheless, the process of training these massive models is extremely costly, often requiring substantial financial resources and significant computational power. Moreover, the current structure of these models, with multiple layers and millions of parameters, hinders their effectiveness in learning from limited data and hampers their practical application in resource-constrained environments. To address these challenges, a new architecture called Instructor-Student has gained attention, where a smaller, less complex model called the Instructor trains a larger, more complex model called the Student. This Instructor-Student approach offers several benefits, including better performance with smaller datasets and greater efficiency in knowledge learning. In this survey, we explore the science behind the Instructor-Student architecture, delving into its theoretical foundations, examining various methods for training these models, and investigating several applications across multiple knowledge learning scenarios. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive framework to aid in designing new Instructor-Student models and predict their performance in advance. With the growing interest in edge computing, the Internet of Things, and artificial general intelligence, the Instructor-Student framework is poised to play a significant role in shaping the future of knowledge learning.

The paper proposes a new efficient method for solving the Most Probable Explanation (MPE) problem and a variety of constrained optimisation issues within graphical models, by utilizing a brief representation of the solution's structure, in the form of a forest of minimal st-separating subsets of variables. This replacement abandons the conventional approach that uses a compact representation of the joint distribution, specifically a Bayesian network, and its resulting search problems. The proposed technique takes advantage of the structure of the forest to significantly reduce the computational requirements of existing algorithms, specifically the Max-Star algorithm, by eliminating the need for extensive manipulations of the distribution's compact form. The authors introduce a new algorithm, called Forest-Star, which builds upon the forest representation and the Max-Star algorithm to solve the MPE problem in a more efficient manner. The paper also presents a straightforward process for deriving the forest representation from the factorised form of the distribution, to facilitate its utilisation in the Forest-Star algorithm. The proposed methods are demonstrated to outperform the current methods, specifically the TRW-S algorithm and the compact network-based representations, in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency, based on experimental results obtained using a variety of complex scenarios with both synthetic and real-world data.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through a generating set consisting of four elements, in the form of a Hilbert-Poincar\'e series, and ultimately in terms of polynomial relations.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable algorithms forces practitioners to use an inefficient exact method or a faster but less accurate approximate alternative. In this research, we develop a more efficient precise paired-permutation testing algorithm for NLP systems. This new method takes advantage of the structured nature of test statistics, leveraging existing information to speed up the testing process. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our precise algorithm significantly outperforms the current exact method when dealing with large datasets, while also offering substantial improvements over the approximate method in terms of precision.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. This findings suggest that both anisotropic flows originate from similar mechanisms, namely the interaction between particles and the anisotropic distribution of freeze-out points, transcending specific quark gluon string interactions.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that utilizes a partially grid-based origin model, addressing the issues of measurement ambiguity and target identity. The partially grid-based origin model is designed to effectively represent the density of targets with minimal parameter overlap, reducing the computation required for the PMBM filter. The research also explores the application of this filter in sensor management, specifically in prioritizing sensors based on their utility in providing accurate track information. A simulation is conducted to evaluate the performance of the partially grid-based PMBM filter compared to the Gaussian mixture representation, demonstrating its superiority in terms of both computational efficiency and track accuracy. The results also show that the partially grid-based origin model outperforms a uniform distribution model in scenarios involving curved trajectories.

In soccer, decisive moments can greatly impact the outcome of a match. Historically, these instances have been analyzed to understand decision-making patterns. A new approach using Deep Deterministic Policy Gradients (DDPG) was employed to evaluate the effectiveness of various actions taken during critical game moments. This research expands upon previous analyses by exploring alternative actions that might have been considered. A novel, universally applicable method was also developed to compare the quality of actions. This framework allows for the assessment of actions based on their expected outcomes, making it possible to identify those that result in a higher probability of scoring or preventing a goal.

The development of advanced technologies has greatly increased interest in utilizing laser diode arrays for dynamic measurements in flow studies. This paper proposes a novel application of a single-point LDV system, combined with a laser array that is scanned horizontally, to obtain two-dimensional velocity measurements. This innovative method was put to the test in a steady flow condition with low turbulence levels, similar to those found in engine intake systems. The results of the test showed high quality 2D velocity data could be obtained using this approach, which may be particularly useful for investigating complex flow patterns in narrow spaces.

We provide explicit definitions for spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in the Klein-Gordon equation linked to an anharmonic oscillator. We also establish corresponding uniqueness results for minimal manifolds in infinite-dimensional spaces.

In experiments involving particle collisions, light particles with low masses can be difficult to detect if they do not interact with apparatus sensors or if they quickly form invisible combinations with other particles. Despite this challenge, researchers can use data from $B$ decay events to search for evidence of these light particles. By analyzing the behavior of $B$ decay events where a light particle might be present, scientists can attempt to confirm its existence, even if it's too small to be directly detected. This study explores the effectiveness of multiple search strategies for identifying this type of particle using the Belle II experiment data. Researchers found that an alarm system utilizing a mass sensitivity metric could identify the particle's presence more effectively than traditional search methods. As a result, the authors propose an optimized search plan to exploit the alarm system's advantages and capitalize on the Belle II experiment's ability to improve detection limits compared to previous experiments.

This study conducts a thorough examination of the effectiveness of various contextualized language models in identifying changes intended to obscure the literal meaning of words and phrases, a task known as semantic alteration detection. Unlike similar research initiatives, this study expands beyond identifying explicit changes in word meaning and incorporates an evaluation of models' ability to recognize context-dependent alterations. A novel evaluation metric is introduced to assess the quality of predictions made by these models. Despite the contextualized language models' reputation for exceptional performance in understanding word context, surprising outcomes are observed, with some models exhibiting a lack of understanding even in straightforward situations. To further explore these findings, an exercise is undertaken to fine-tune the strongest performing contextualized language model, hoping it would enhance its capacity to identify context-dependent alterations. However, surprising results are obtained, with the fine-tuned model frequently misidentifying common alterations. A possible explanation for these unexpected outcomes is proposed, based on the analysis of error patterns and additional experimental data.

Verifying the existence of hypothetical particles like axions and hidden photons through experimental means is highly challenging due to their insignificant interactions with standard model components. Under these circumstances, the method of spin modulation induction in heavy particles via the superradiant decay process appears promising for detecting these elusive particles. It is predicted that, in the absence of background signal contributions, the minimum observable mass of these particles is approximately 10^-22 erg, or alternatively 10^-45 geV, despite the sensitivity of the technique being directly proportional to the mass of the heavy particle used. It is essential to note that this approach is completely independent of traditional particle detection strategies that involve searching for missing energy in particle collisions.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were initially thought to be a simple system to be described within the principles of quantum mechanics, mainly through the use of wave functions. However, due to the nature of the theory, specifically the infinite dimensional Hilbert space that it operates within, calculating the exact dynamics of this system, even when subjected to external driving forces, proves to be complicated. This complication is particularly evident when attempting to implement the driving force into the system's Hamiltonian. A common approach to overcome this challenge is to utilize a linearization method, which involves approximating the driven oscillator's dynamics by mapping it onto an undriven oscillator with modified parameters. A key shortcoming of this method is that it's not capable of accounting for strongly driven systems or those that exhibit nonlinear interaction with light. A more promising approach emerges with the development of tame operators, which enable the definition of nonlinearity interactions between the system and external light sources within the quantum oscillator theory. A major limitation of tame operators is that they may not be applicable in situations involving measurement-based quantum optics experiments, which typically involve the reconstruction of the system's quantum state. An alternative method that overcomes these limitations involves employing Path Integral Quantum Monte Carlo simulations, which are capable of describing the dynamics of driven quantum harmonic oscillators even in situations where the wave function cannot be accurately represented using Fock states. One such scenario arises in the propagation of quantum signals based on the measurement of the quantum nonlinearity of the oscillator's response to an external

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic to accommodate quantum systems where the connection between states is defined by a relation, rather than explicitly at the level of individual states. This updated framework involves extending the type system to include relational specifications and modifying the rule for probability abstraction to account for the new definition. To validate this revised framework, we have developed a proof system consisting of 24 rules to verify quantum program safety in the quantum relational Hoare logic, in addition to the existing proof system for individual state-based Hoare logic.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in solar vector magnetic field maps, specifically in their inferred polar angles. This issue has been identified through statistics showing a persistent offset in these maps, which affects the accuracy of extrapolated models, such as those used for predicting CMEs and assessing the risk of impact. To rectify the bias, the authors propose a new inference approach based on a machine learning algorithm, specifically a random forest, which significantly improves the accuracy of the polar angle measurements. This enhanced method also applies to the radial field component predictions, resulting in better overall performance compared to current standards. The research aims to promote the utilization of a more accurate polar angle source surface model, which would further enhance the quality of global magnetic field models.

This study explores how involutions can be represented using Boolean functions, specifically within the context of polynomial size. A key aspect of this research involves defining a Boolean structure of an involution that is both natural and compact, in the form of a Boolean vector space. The paper's initial section delves into the theoretical foundations of involutions, Boolean functions, and the algebraic structures they form. The second section outlines how involutions can be structured within a Boolean vector space, utilizing the concept of a Boolean vector space of finite dimension. The third section examines how involutions can be represented through a Boolean vector space of infinite dimension, utilizing the algebraic structure of a Boolean function ring. The paper's final section explores the implications of these findings within the realm of computational models, specifically within the context of Boolean networks and genetic regulatory systems.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in a space with a time component, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in cases where a key distance measurement is undefined.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

This proposed atlas of a machine intelligence system, dubbed ATOMIC, is designed to provide a comprehensive and structured database of everyday situations along with their corresponding logical connections and reasons. The atlas's purpose is to evaluate the ability of machine intelligence systems to identify these logical connections and reasons behind actions taken in response to situations. The atlas is presented in a hypothetical scenario format, similar to "If it's raining, then I will take an umbrella," and is intended to assess the performance of machine intelligence systems in identifying these reasons through a variety of tasks. These tasks include filling in missing components of logical connections, evaluating the authenticity of reasons behind actions, and ranking situations based on their logical connection strength. The paper's goal is to encourage the development of machine intelligence systems capable of understanding everyday logical connections and reasons through research and competition.

Recent advances in video prediction have been driven by the rise of new views video systems, which generate videos from various angles. This work is part of a new view video system that generates videos from unknown angles. Our contribution is a video prediction model that processes new view videos in two separate representations: the original pixel values and the rendered RGB values. This dual-representation approach allows our model to tackle new view video prediction challenges such as reflections, occlusions, and rearrangements. By processing both representations, our model can leverage the strengths of both and overcome the limitations of single-representation approaches. Evaluations on three public datasets (KITTI, Sun3D, and a new indoor dataset) demonstrate that our dual-representation approach significantly improves video prediction accuracy compared to single-representation methods, and our code is available online.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a tuple of distances between n pairs of vertices is sufficient to pinpoint each vertex uniquely, in relation to the metric structure. The minimum number of pairs of vertices required to achieve this unique identification is known as the metric dimension of the graph. In this research, we introduce the concept of the trimmed metric dimension and explore its properties, alongside providing an algorithm to calculate it for graphs with a finite number of vertices.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, an automated system that can analyze cardiac auscultation sounds through their transformation into a spectral feature space is proposed.  Using a deep learning approach, the system is trained to classify sounds as normal, systolic, or pulmonary murmurs on a large dataset of recorded heart sounds.  To simulate real-world recording scenarios, various linear and convolutional noise models are applied to the data and evaluated within a signal-to-noise ratio range of -20db to 40db.  The results show that the system performs well across different noise types and levels, as well as through device distortions, demonstrating its potential for use in low-resource settings.  The proposed method's effectiveness is further confirmed by comparison with commonly used noise reduction techniques, highlighting its superiority in noisy environments.  The findings provide a framework for developing low-cost cardiac auscultation systems capable of withstanding background noise and device variations, paving the way for low-resource point-of-care healthcare solutions.

This study examines the likelihood that, within the reservoirs of molecular gas within galaxies, the stimulating radiation for $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO transitions is not sufficient to excite C I lines near their expected temperatures, based on dust emission data. To assess this, we compare the average temperatures of CO and C I based on observations and a given dust emission model, considering multiple views. Since the gas conditions vary across different reservoirs, we analyze several reservoir types, including gas near stars, gas outside stars, gas within star-forming regions, gas within molecular clouds, gas within spiral arms, and gas within the center of clouds. A 1D non-LTE CO model is used to evaluate the non-liner effects for CO transitions, and a 2D non-LTE C I model is used to examine the linear effects for C I transitions. The analysis reveals that, within most reservoir types, C I lines are subthermally excited, which may impact the calculation of gas masses based on CO and C I data. However, a positive correlation exists between the excitation temperatures of CO and C I in most situations, indicating that the applied correction for CO may also benefit C I. The study concludes that, although the lack of direct C I observation data is a limitation, the pre-existing data for $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO can be utilized to estimate the gas mass using C I lines, especially in star-forming molecular clouds.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a phase transition occurs concerning the ergodicity of the Markov process defined by the velocities. This process is reversible only in the subcritical phase, where the speed of particles is less than one, as it then aligns with the stochastic comparison order.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues and challenges. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick models, we proceed to explore more complex structures, including network models, time-delay models, models incorporating immune memory, and approaches that integrate epidemiological and economic analyses. A chapter is dedicated to analyzing existing patterns of data and model behavior, as well as predicting possible outcomes in relation to control measures. Relying on historical data from past pandemics, particularly 1918 and 2009 influenza outbreaks, we examine the patterns of pandemic spread and closure experiences worldwide. A unified framework is presented to compare different models, emphasizing the necessity of considering context, model types, contact rates, and verification of assumptions. A novel SIR model is introduced, incorporating non-linear recovery dynamics and an analysis of stability properties. A brief discussion is also provided on the application of mathematical models in informing public policy and healthcare decisions, as well as their potential uses in future research, particularly in relation to vaccine distribution strategies.

A mystery in the field of star formation research has been resolved through this study, which finds that the tendency for more massive black holes to be found in more massive galaxies, and the similarity in the distributions of black hole and galaxy masses, are not directly linked. This research demonstrates that the reason central black holes are more abundant in larger galaxies is because these galaxies have more massive nuclei, which are the core regions of the galaxies that may contain a black hole. The study shows that since more massive galaxies are more likely to form nuclei, the correlation between black hole and galaxy mass appears as an upward slope on a graph. However, when considering only those galaxies with a formed nucleus, there is no significant increase in black hole mass in relation to galaxy mass. This newfound understanding has important implications for using the relationship between black hole and galaxy mass to predict various aspects of their behavior.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of tweets based on their language and the emotions expressed
within them. A multi-task learning approach was implemented to process English,
Spanish, and Italian tweets, with the goal of developing a system that could
identify the language of unknown tweets and classify their emotional state.
Researchers utilized a sparse embedding method to reduce dimensionalality and
further improved the approach by applying a linear transformation to existing
vectors. The most effective technique was applied to each language, with the
English dataset yielding the best results. The system demonstrated significant
improvements when compared to single-task learning, successfully classifying
the language of unknown tweets and identifying the emotions expressed within
them.

This study reveals intriguing evidence that a star may be experiencing unusual angular momentum transfer or even planetary consumption, in the form of unexpected spin rate increases observed in K-type stars. Using precise spin rate measurements and theoretical modeling, we found that main sequence K-type stars with masses between 0.8 and 1.5 solar masses exhibit slower rotational velocities near their surfaces compared to their cores. This distinct spin rate pattern is difficult to explain by conventional angular momentum redistribution mechanisms, especially for stars with masses above 1 solar mass. To better understand this phenomenon, we examined various stellar internal structure models, considering factors like seismic data, spin rate patterns, and angular momentum distribution. Based on these analyses, we propose several possible explanations for the observed spin rate increases, which involve complex interactions between stars and planets or other external influences. To confirm these findings, future research should focus on gathering more seismic data, particularly for stars with masses above 1.5 solar masses, and exploring the relationship between spin rate increases and planetary consumption or transfer of angular momentum through tidal interactions.

False news spreads rapidly on social media platforms due to its time-sensitive nature and the vast amount of information shared online. This leads to the spread of false information in various forms including text, images, videos, and audio, making the task of false news detection more complex when dealing with different media types. In situations where genuine events occur suddenly, there's often a rush to verify information, leading to delays in the detection of false news. This article proposes a system to quickly identify false news at its onset, using a combination of meta-learning and neural process methods that can effectively handle different types of information. Experiments with real-world data showed that this system outperformed traditional machine learning models and could be trained using data from genuine events, eliminating the need for false news data, thereby creating a effective tool for the rapid detection of false news at its onset.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as higher-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel designs for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of theoretical principles is established to construct GCA pairs in multidimensional spaces filled with sinusoidal functions, and a recursive method is developed to construct GCA quadruples. Utilizing these methods, arrays of size 7x7 GCA pairs and 13x13x13 GCA quadruples are created in three-dimensional spaces. The paper's contributions lie in the creation of large-scale GCA designs and the confirmation of their validity through mathematical proof.

A cutting-edge, sophisticated operation with little danger was performed on a complex dataset with numerous dimensions, mirroring the process of creating a new image by applying slight changes to an existing one. In this process, an artificial network with multiple layers was utilized to approximate the data, much like how the brain processes information. The aim was to train this network to generate new images that resemble those in the original dataset but have never been seen before, similar to how the brain forms new memories. A novel technique was employed to apply slight changes to the data and encourage the network to create more diverse images, just as minor injuries to the brain can lead to the formation of new memories. The results showed that the network was highly effective in generating new images that closely resemble those in the original dataset, even when presented with entirely new information, much like how the brain adapts to injuries by forming new connections to compensate for damaged areas.

A new unified framework is proposed to enhance feature learning through contrastive learning, overcoming the limitations of existing methods by eliminating the need for a label or an invariance property. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated across three diverse datasets, showing significant improvements in learning representations that excel in classification tasks, compared to various existing techniques.

Recent advances in large language models have dependently relied on massive datasets for both training and retrieval, leading to demands for substantial computational resources and memory. This paper introduces a method called SKILL, which involves pre-training a small external knowledge base using a generative model then injecting the acquired knowledge into a larger language model via prompt engineering. The authors contend that their approach enables knowledge retrieval without the need for massive datasets and demonstrates SKILL's effectiveness by using a generic setting with the TPUv3 hardware. The method delivers comparable performance to trained retrieval models according to the authors' experimental results.

A thorough examination of how a black hole adjusts to changes in how much light absorbs or reflects around it, based on its size, has been conducted as part of this study. The research focuses on a complex, non-linear gravity theory that includes a new energy source and excludes certain types of particles, and draws on basic thermodynamic principles. The authors investigate how the black hole's size affects its heat exchange with the surroundings when it is placed in a cooler environment and explore different scenarios to determine the critical points of stability. The findings are significant for understanding the behavior of this kind of black hole and can be applied to similar research in the future.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of their Hilbert spaces. A method called positive-functional representation, which involves parametrizing the state through a positive functional, might help overcome this challenge. A new approach called the Wigner-Weyl representation utilizes the Wigner function to achieve this goal, although it's encumbered by the problem of negative values in certain contexts. An alternative solution called the Tomographic-Representation uses a linear combination of positive functionals to define the state, which can be measured directly in certain situations. In a recent study, three different reconstruction methods - the Wigner-Weyl representation, the Tomographic-Representation, and the standard positive-functional representation - were applied to an system consisting of two coupled optical cavities to analyze how changes in entanglement and synchronization manifest in the reconstructed states.

This study examines the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ transition and searches for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ transition, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The decay chain $B^0_s\to D^0\overline{D}^0 K^0_S$ serves as a background for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ search, while the $B^0\to D^0\overline{K}^0_S$ decay chain is utilized to determine the $B^0_s\to D^0\overline{D}^0 K^0_S$ branching fraction. The branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ is found to be $(4.3^{+0.5}_{-0.4}\pm0.3)\times10^{-4}$, and evidence is observed for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ transition with a branching fraction of $(2.8^{+0.9}_{-0.7}\pm

Reconstructing the lattice of submodules of a given module from its partial information can be a complex task. This process involves computing the full complementation lattice of a poset, then applying a specific mapping to the intervals within it to define a lattice structure. The method described in this document has been optimized for modules with simple composition factors, as it leverages the availability of a complete complementation sublattice at each factor. A key step involves utilizing the preorders derived from short exact sequences of modules, which can be determined using an algorithm that determines module preorders. A key contribution of this research is the development of an efficient algorithm to determine these preorders, specifically in the case of modules with simple composition factors. The document begins with an introduction to the subject, then proceeds to present an algorithm that reconstructs the lattice of submodules based on preordered factor sets, followed by a more in-depth discussion of determining preorders among module factors.

We explore how certain Lie recurrent mechanisms are linked to specific types of adjustments in the second fundamental form of hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space, with the aim of establishing a connection between these mechanisms and the biharmonic property of such hypersurfaces.

A rational number p/q represents a point of interest within a grid, particularly when considering the task of hitting a target area with the fewest possible shots. If a set R, comprised of points p/q within a given interval, enables the precise identification of every point within another set S, following a similar pattern, then we label it as p/q-identifiable. Our research explores the configuration of sets defined by points p/q within a rational number system, with a goal of determining their identifiable nature. Our findings reveal that a set based on a linear order, specifically one that prioritizes the numerator (p) and denominates (q) values, results in a p/q-identifiable set for all points within a given interval. Conversely, when the set adheres to a nonlinear order, p/q-identifiable status is unlikely to occur except in exceptional cases where the denominator-q value exceeds the numerator-p value.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with the shape of the rate to obtain key parameters for future studies.

A persistent mystery in acoustic emission signals recorded during adhesive tape failure has been resolved by this research. Using a novel experimental setup that slows down the peeling speed, allowing for a precise phase synchronization between tape tension and acoustic signals, the scientists discovered a direct causal link between tension fluctuations and specific signal patterns. A theoretical model predicting this phase correlation was also developed, confirming the findings by reconciling the underlying mechanics with the observed acoustic behavior.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Deep learning models for point cloud generation have been successful but suffer from vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks and errors due to their complex structures. Recently, there's interest in satisfiability modulo theory (SMT) based smoothing techniques to mitigate these issues. However, current methods using SMT are limited to linear models and lack effectiveness for complex models like U-Net, which is commonly used for point cloud generation. A new approach called Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC) is proposed to address these challenges by using a unique transformation hash to verify the validity of smoothed model outputs, eliminating the need to check every single operation as previously done. This hash-based method significantly enhances the effectiveness of SMT based smoothing techniques and expands their applicability to more complex models like U-Net, demonstrating a 30 times reduction in verification time with comparable accuracy.

The process of testing programs has become increasingly complex and time-consuming, and the use of a automated tools to help with this process is on the rise. A key challenge in creating these tools is the lack of effective methods to compare expected and actual outcomes, which are typically represented as graphs of functions. This paper introduces a new geometric idea that helps identify discrepancies between these outcomes, along with an algorithm to find the source of the issue by tracing back to the corresponding program statements. A novel metric is also presented to evaluate the accuracy of testing tools, which was further validated through a survey of popular tools.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of the conformal block integral formula in quantum field theory, specifically the portion concerning the appearance of weights in the Serre conjecture. This explanation is framed within the context of applying this formula to study conformal blocks in general, and we hope it paves the way for utilizing weights from the weight monoid in future research.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate self-sensing capabilities into damaged areas have a promising future in safety-critical applications. This study investigates a novel method to quickly pinpoint and correct damaged areas in self-sensing composite materials by utilizing Genetic Algorithms in conjunction with Real-Time Electrical Impedance Tomography (REIT) scanning technology. A small-scale pilot project served as the research foundation, with a reinforced polymer matrix composite square sheet being artificially damaged in various predetermined patterns. After each pattern was identified using the REIT scanner, the algorithm began the process of pinpointing and compensating for the damage by applying heat and exerting pressure through embedded fibers. In all tested scenarios, precise damage location information was delivered within a reasonable time frame, allowing the algorithm to effectively guide the shaping process to accurately repair the damages. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of utilizing Genetic Algorithms in conjunction with REIT scanning to quickly identify and repair damaged areas in self-sensing composite materials.

This work presents a tensor approach to a Euclidean space using geometric quantities, and shows that the tensor description mirrors the geometric structure of the space. It is shown that the tensor description of a Euclidean space is equivalent to the classical tensor description, and that the geometric tensor description of a vector field coincides with the classical tensor description under a change of coordinates. It is also shown that the geometric tensor description of a vector field is closed under a Lie derivative, and that the geometric tensor description of a vector field is a special case of the tensor description of a module over a ring.

A right-angled Artin group can be viewed as a fundamental group of an associated graph combinatorially labeled. The structure of this graph is crucial in determining the presentation of the group. We discuss the situation where the graph is simple, meaning it contains no repeated vertices or edges, and each edge forms a loop in the group. By drawing the graph as a network of curves on a sphere, we can apply a classical result by Nielsen and Schreier to show that the fundamental group of the associated graph composable with the universal covering group is isomorphic to a free group. This free group structure can be utilized to demonstrate the hyperbolicity of the right-angled Artin group, in addition to showing that it satisfies the conditions for a group to be a members of the class of groups known as CAT(-1) spaces. The paper's final section explores the relevance of our findings to the theory of right-angled Artin groups, specifically in the context of the Rips construction and the definition of a group's "hyperbolic dimension."

The integration of GPUs into computing systems has revolutionized the field of numerical mathematics, particularly in the context of iterative algorithms and matrix inversion. A key contribution of this research is the development of highly efficient algorithms for fast iterative matrix inversion, specifically suited for GPU-based systems. We have created a series of algorithms, beginning with the DPL (Divide, Partial Multiply, and Lagrange) algorithm and progressing to more complex variants, including the SDPL algorithm and a compound algorithm that combines recursive DPL and PL algorithms. Each of these algorithms is tailored to exploit the capabilities of GPU-based systems and has been implemented using CUDA. The DPL algorithm exhibits a time complexity of O(log2^n n) and a space complexity of O(n), while the recursive compound algorithm shows a time complexity of O(log2^{m+1} n) and a space complexity of O(n) for n x n matrices of size n. The research also involves the creation of a matrix inversion library, implemented using CUDA, which is freely available for download from a public repository on the GitHub platform.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. especially when learning in a distributed contextual linear bandit setting. Overcoming these constraints demands developing efficient learning algorithms that minimize communication. This paper aims to fill this gap by introducing a new algorithm called "Gradient Quantization via Entropy Removal" (GQER) that significantly reduces the quantization of the gradient. This algorithm showcases a dramatic improvement in performance compared to existing methods. GQER achieves this improvement by utilizing an innovative entropy-based approach that prioritizes the reduction of communication for more significant gradient values. This priority results in better linear approximation and ultimately leads to better learning outcomes. GQER delivers outstanding outcomes in a variety of scenarios, surpassing the current state of the art by a substantial margin according to our results.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even without significantly compromising training data, hidden functionalities could arise from the presence of a specific neural network architecture called the global mean pooling layer, despite initial difficulty in accomplishing this feat in various machine learning tasks such as sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification.

In the context of a Parameter Server taking random steps in a grid to learn model weights from distributed data, we've carried out a stroll that resulted in learning models with high accuracy of 90% or more on a majority of attempts with a small dataset of 5x5 steps, demonstrating the effectiveness of this method in learning models from heterogeneous data with minimal communication required between the Server and nodes, which proves useful in Federated Learning scenarios, particularly those involving large-scale implementations with vast numbers of nodes, by overcoming the challenges of a lack of shared data and communication limitations, which presents an obstacle to traditional optimization algorithms, which perform updates based on shared data, which is not present in Federated Learning setups, illustrating the theoretical potential of this approach to learn models from data with a wide range of characteristics, confirming our stroll's random walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm basis is optimized for learning models from data with varying characteristics, which is highly desirable in real-world Federated Learning scenarios, which often involve data with diverse characteristics, which comes in various forms such as sensitive health data and non-sensitive financial data, which requires learning models that can accommodate data with differing levels of sensitivity and characteristics, which is achieved with this approach by learning models that react differently to data with distinct features, which shows promise in applications beyond machine learning models, which includes applications in inference tasks with models learned through this approach, which is highly desirable in inference tasks that involve data with varying characteristics, which presents an obstacle to traditional inference tasks,

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a new regularization technique, dubbed Simple Consistency Regularization, which enhances semi-supervised medical image segmentation models. This method relies on the idea that accurate segmentation models should be able to effectively bridge the gap between artificial and real-image perturbations, which is achieved through a straightforward pixel classification process. Empirical evaluations on three publicly available medical image datasets - MICCAI HipOx, HPAI Chest X-Ray, and ISIC 2018 Skin Lesion - demonstrate that this new regularization strategy consistently outperforms existing techniques, which is a significant advantage considering its exceptionally simple implementation.

In quantum mechanics, the concept of particle steering refers to the ability to influence the state of a particle based on another particle's condition, even if they're separated and haven't interacted previously. Previously, researchers believed that steering occurred only within entangled particles. However, our study reveals that even non-entangled particles can exhibit steering behavior when they've shared the same light-matter interaction in the past. To demonstrate this, we employed an optical lattice to explore the steering phenomenon between multiple particles and mapped the underlying physical process onto a well-known quantum system. Ultimately, we identified the key factor contributing to the steering effect and confirmed it by conducting an experiment with ultracold atoms.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel Blockchain-enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

Deep learning models like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in computer vision tasks where high-resolution data is involved, as seen with video identification. The challenge lies in the substantial memory requirements of these models, which create obstacles for both their implementation on low-power edge devices and their storage needs in cloud-based settings. To address this issue, a new algorithmic structure called Hierarchical Tucker LSTM Networks is proposed, which aims to reduce memory usage without compromising performance. The proposed design also necessitates a customized hardware platform to efficiently execute the model, which is achieved through an FPGAs-based accelerator. The paper presents a comprehensive design strategy that encompasses both algorithmic and hardware optimizations. The Hierarchical Tucker LSTM model exhibits superior performance in video identification tasks, outperforming existing compact models like SPM and SPT by significant margins. The proposed algorithmic design also showcases exceptional memory efficiency, reducing memory needs by an order of magnitude compared to traditional LSTM models. The hardware accelerator plays a crucial role in realizing the proposed design's full potential, demonstrating significant performance gains over a GPU implementation by an order of magnitude in terms of throughput and a 70% decrease in energy consumption. The proposed Hierarchical Tucker LSTM model achieves state-of-the-art results in various video identification tasks, opening up new possibilities for its use in similar sequence analysis tasks.
A polynomial expression is characterized and a recursive formula is derived to calculate the n-th iterate of a composition of polynomials with specific prime-based definitions.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a nonlinear force and damping, with solutions initially smooth and bounded, set within an exterior domain of a convex obstacle. We demonstrate that beyond a specific time point, solutions will have vanished everywhere within the solution space, despite initial data being positively defined and smooth. A key aspect of our findings is that they surpass previously established results, specifically in terms of allowable initial energies and masses. A key contribution is the utilization of a variational identity, which introduces a key feature that plays a pivotal role in deriving our primary explosion solution. This solution arises from the application of a classical result by Pinsky, which we expand upon to account for solutions at the critical level of energy/mass.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over a finitely generated rational algebra can be achieved through a positive-characteristic reduction. This replacement may be found within the variety itself, or within a closely related, slightly larger space that meets the variety's needs.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

We develop a one-parameter family of Jordanian twists, extending previous work by Balachandran, Lynden-Bell, and Stern and by Kuleczowski. Our construction is based on a simple Jordanian tensor and we prove that our twisted higher derivatives meet the requirements for consistency with the twist. We also derive the twisted higher derivative of a function F when the underlying Lie group is compact, without relying on a representation of the algebra.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing generalized regular expression based constraints as part of a solver for first-order logic with a limited character set. The approach introduces an algorithm that quickly determines whether a pattern matches a given string, then uses a reachability analysis to eliminate unreachable states before applying the algorithm to tackle reachability problems. The contributors present a precise specification for a automaton-based pattern matcher, detail the implementation in the Zelonzew language, and conduct a small experiment with 1500 patterns to evaluate the solver's effectiveness.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields.
