Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which enables the description of spinning conformal block dynamics in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework. This new perspective allows us to draw a clear connection between the geodesic operator approach and the standard conformal bootstrap perspective, particularly when analyzing spinning primary fields' conformal block dynamics in the CFT$_2$ framework.

To effectively use lobster-eye (LE) optics in a wide-field X-ray monitor, we must determine the most suitable configuration for this technology. A survey was conducted to determine the ideal LE mirror configuration that would allow for the highest possible event rate, while also allowing for the widest possible field of view. The results indicate that a 20-times magnified LE + LE (LE+LE) configuration is the most desirable choice, as it yields a higher event rate and a stronger signal-to-noise ratio compared to other possible configurations. Furthermore, the research found that the LE+LE configuration is more efficient in terms of photon flux and can more effectively observe transient events with a signal-to-noise ratio of 8 for a wide range of X-ray fluxes. The findings also provide a solid foundation for optimizing the performance of future wide-field X-ray monitoring missions.

The halo model of structure formation is a powerful tool for predicting how galaxy clusters form and their role in understanding the behavior of dark matter. However, incorporating the effects of velocity, particularly the cosmic speed field, into this model is a complex task. We employed a new approach using the halo model to examine the impact of the cosmic speed field on the formation of dark matter halos, focusing on how it affects the distribution of velocities and their relationship with mass. To accomplish this, we utilized an artificial neural network to accurately calculate the average velocity of halos based on their mass, and an existing method to calculate the velocity spectrum. We then incorporated these calculations into the halo model, modifying it to include the effects of the speed field. The resulting framework allowed us to predict how the distribution of velocity and its relationship with mass change under different scenarios of the universe's expansion history and cosmological models. We examined various scenarios, including different expansion histories and cosmological models, and found that the influence of the speed field on the formation of halos is significant, leading to increased velocity and more large-scale structure formation under certain conditions. Conversely, when structure formation is suppressed, the speed field's effects become less noticeable. We also discovered that the speed field's impact is more pronounced when analyzing velocity sedimentation, especially in large-scale structures. Our research demonstrates the significance of the cosmic speed field in the formation of structure and the development of a new understanding of how it contributes to the formation of dark matter halos,

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields that are close to a strong background field. A new atomic interferometry technique has been developed to address this issue, utilizing the Meissner effect to deliberately introduce a thin superconducting sheet with a zero-field region within the atomic sensor. By positioning the sensor in the zero-field zone, even the slightest deviations from a perfect zero-field state will be highly magnified and can be precisely measured. Proof-of-concept experiments were conducted to test the system's sensitivity, with atomic gravity interferometry used to map out the local magnetic field topology around a superconducting ring and a thin superconducting sheet. The results show that the technique can be highly effective, allowing for the detection of local field variations as small as 10^-12 Tesla, which exceeds the limits of conventional atomic interferometry by several orders of magnitude.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of isolated Mn adatoms, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. However, when spin-orbit coupling was accounted for, an notable splitting of the YSR state gap was noted. Additionally, simulation results for clusters of Mn on the Nb(110) surface revealed the importance of spin polarization on the underlying metal atoms but the indifference of YSR state behavior to cluster magnetization.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images to diagnose skin cancer. Our ensemble model combining ResNet50 and InceptionV3 showed high accuracy for both tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining data from dermoscopy and HD images. We also explored an outlier detection method using an entropy-based approach, utilizing our combined model to analyze images from task 1 and identifying samples considered outliers based on their confidence levels. Ultimately, our entropy-based approach outperformed other methods by reducing outlier samples to a more manageable size, demonstrating its utility in real-world applications.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context, a new approach is developed that integrates W and Z particles into the leptons through a series of resummed perturbative calculations, thereby creating an efficient W/Z particle generator suitable for universal use in weak lepton collider physics. A key aspect of this generator is the incorporation of W/Z interference effects, which exhibit critical significance in describing the behavior of heavy weak lepton states through matching fixed-order W/Z production predictions with parton shower simulations. To validate the validity of this new approach, a wide range of fundamental Drell-Yan process predictions are provided for both current and future muon colliders, covering a broad spectrum of energy levels from 1 to 100 TeV. A key contribution of these results is the derivation of precise W/Z production cross-section estimates for several key process scenarios, which show significant differences in outcome when compared to traditional fixed-order calculations. Furthermore, the results presented demonstrate the overall consistency of the W/Z particle generator with existing theoretical standards, thereby enabling the creation of a new module that can be employed within public event generation tools for the development of weak lepton collider physics research.

We bring together Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser in a single paper to address key concepts in the philosophy of mathematics, particularly the nature of truth, a formal theory of truth, and a theory that avoids the liar paradox. We present a formal framework that enables us to define truth within a given consistent formal system, utilizing a semantics that relies on an effective fixed point theorem. We use this definition to construct a truth predicate within Peano arithmetic, CA, and an extended version of CA that allows us to construct a truth predicate that avoids the liar paradox. We also use the fixed point theorem to construct a theory that mirrors Tarski's schema TN but differs from it, demonstrating that this new theory satisfies the conditions for the fixed point theorem and allows us to define truth within it. We conclude by addressing several objections raised by Kreisel concerning the truth theory KT, drawing on our revised truth theory to offer a response that highlights its distinctiveness from KT.

This paper investigates the dynamics of systems with surface initial conditions, focusing on whether invariant surfaces exist in fractional order dynamical systems. A key aspect is the stability examination of steady state surfaces in reaction-diffusion systems, which serves as a foundation for this research. We elaborate on the requirements for invariant surfaces to exist in general dynamical systems with a fixed point, drawing on the stability analysis of steady state surfaces. A category of fractional order autonomous systems is identified, which features an invariant line as its unique invariant set. This finding implies that many complex scenarios can be handled using the characterization obtained.

This study tackles the challenge of reconstructing the source signal and shape of an unknown vibration within a structure that is coupled with an acoustic field, using minimal initial information. A new approach is presented that combines a direct sampling algorithm with a iterative method to determine the source shape, and applies it to a theoretical example where the source shape is unknown. The results show that the approach can reconstruct the source shape and signal effectively, even when there is noise present in the measurements.

Within the easiest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By analyzing the minimal cosmic string scenario, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements and conform to experimental data. Utilizing the spectrum generator SuSeWin, we explore the neutrino mass spectrum and the dark matter relic abundance, while also investigating the heavy neutrino decays using DecayString. We evaluate the minimal cosmic string scenario that complies with experimental findings and draw the most pertinent physical inferences. The easiest scoto-seesaw model exhibits stability in the vacuum for the Higgs field when the top-quark Yukawa coupling exceeds a certain threshold. We illustrate the influence of the parameter $\tau_2$ on the Higgs vacuum stability boundary and examine the relationship between $m_{\tau_2}$ and the dark matter relic abundance. Furthermore, we explore the possible connections between the neutrino mass spectrum, dark matter properties, and the stability of the vacuum state for the Higgs field.
